sharedText: and came and dwelt in the
reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and a six-word run, and it is narrative connective tissue. Genesis 13:18 is Abram moving his tent to the plain of Mamre and building an altar; Ether 8:2 is a son who has rebelled against his father going to live in the land of Heth before buying half a kingdom with flattery. The shared string is 'and came and dwelt in the', which is how the King James Bible says that somebody moved house — it does the same work at Genesis 13:18, and the Book of Mormon uses relocation formulas of this kind continuously through the Jaredite king-list. Nothing of Abram's altar, tent, or promise is present, and no content word beyond the verbs is shared.

Already excluded at Ether 7:4 on the same four-word run and for the same reason; the entry is repeated here because the machine proposes it again and a reader working verse by verse will meet it again. Matthew 10:35 is Christ describing the division his coming makes within households — the man set at variance against his father is being separated by loyalty to Christ, and the saying is a warning about the cost of discipleship. Ether 8:2 is a prince raising a rebellion to depose and imprison his own father for the kingdom. The verbal overlap is the preposition and the kinship noun; the senses have nothing in common.

This one is genuinely tempting and worth the space. Jeremiah 17:11 is the KJV's proverb about ill-gotten power: 'so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool.' Ether 8 is precisely a story about getting a kingdom not by right, and 8:4 says that Omer 'was in captivity the half of his days' — a life measured out in halves, in a chapter whose other half-measure is the half of the kingdom. But the sense is inverted at the decisive point. In Jeremiah the man whose days are cut in half is the one who took what was not his; in Ether 8:4 the man whose days are halved is the rightful king who was robbed, and the usurper Jared keeps his gains until his own daughter's plot unmakes them. If Jeremiah 17:11 stood behind any verse of this chapter it would have to stand behind Jared, and it does not stand behind Jared verbally either. Recorded so that a reader who notices the proverb is told the catalogue noticed it and declined it.

sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
reason: A nine-word run, the longest in the chapter, and entirely covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5. 'And it came to pass that when they had' is the Book of Mormon's ordinary narrative hinge; Amos 7:2's continuation is locusts finishing the grass of the land and the prophet interceding for Jacob, and Ether 8:6 is a night battle ending in a plea for a life. Listed rather than passed over in silence only because its length makes it the top-ranked candidate for the verse and a reader may wonder why it is not a link.

A four-word run with opposed referents. In Acts 9:29 the Grecians go about to slay Saul because he disputes boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and the narrative's sympathy is entirely with the intended victim, who escapes to Tarsus. In Ether 8:6 the men about to slay Jared are his own brothers putting down an armed rebellion against their father, and the narrative's judgment falls on the man whose life is spared: sparing him is what allows everything in the rest of the chapter to happen. The phrase is the KJV's ordinary way of saying that a killing was imminent.

A rarity coincidence worth registering and not worth cataloguing. 'His kinsfolks' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 16:11 and 2 Kings 10:11, and both are dynastic massacres — Zimri destroying the house of Baasha, Jehu destroying the house of Ahab, in each case killing the dead king's kinsfolk along with his priests and his great men. Ether 8:13 gathers 'all his kinsfolks' into a house to plot a dynastic massacre, which makes the coincidence arresting: the same rare noun, the same political operation, in the same three verses of the King James Bible. But the roles are exactly reversed. In Kings the kinsfolk are the victims of the purge; in Ether they are its instrument, and they survive it. Since the word is one noun and the reversal is total, the case cannot be argued as dependence. The Judges 15:12 link at this verse is where the verbal evidence actually is.

'Whoso should divulge whatsoever thing Akish made known unto them, the same should lose his life.' 'Shall lose his life' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 8:35 and Luke 17:33, and 'lose his life' in four, all four of them the same saying of Jesus about losing one's life for his sake and finding it. The construction Ether uses even keeps Mark's resumptive pronoun — 'the same shall save it' / 'the same should lose his life'. It is refused because the saying is a paradox about voluntary self-loss for the gospel's sake and Ether 8:14 is a penalty clause in a murder contract: the life lost is taken by the conspirators, not laid down, and it is lost for keeping a secret rather than for confessing Christ. Recorded because the shared string is genuinely rare and a careful reader could be caught by it. The oath's real source is at Matthew 5:34-36, catalogued as a link on this verse.

'They were kept up by the power of the devil … to keep them in darkness.' Acts 26:18 is the KJV's one verse joining the two ideas: Paul is sent 'to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God'. The conjunction of darkness with a satanic power is thus not common KJV property, and the temptation to link is real. But 'power of the devil' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses — the KJV says 'power of Satan' — and nothing else of Acts 26:18 is present: no eyes opened, no turning, no forgiveness, no inheritance. What Ether 8:16 has is the Book of Mormon's own standing idiom for the secret combinations, 'works of darkness' and the devil's power, which runs from 2 Nephi 9:9 through Helaman 6:28-30 and reaches this verse from inside the book. Declined at any confidence for want of verbal contact.

'Neither doth he will that man should shed blood, but in all things hath forbidden it, from the beginning of man.' The claim being made is a claim about Genesis — that the shedding of human blood was prohibited from the outset — and the KJV states the prohibition once, at Genesis 9:6, 'Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.' That verse is the Bible's foundational homicide statute, it binds a pre-Israelite world, and this catalogue has already used it as the source of Nephi's objection at 1 Nephi 4:10, where the wording was genuinely reproduced. Here it is not. 'Should shed blood' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses; 'sheddeth man' is a Genesis 9:6 singleton and Ether does not have it; the image of God, the talionic clause, and Noah are all absent. And the doctrine does not quite fit either: Genesis 9:6 is given after the flood, whereas Ether 8:19 dates the prohibition 'from the beginning of man', which is Helaman 6:29's phrase and the Book of Mormon's own antediluvian chronology of the secret combinations. Refused as a link and recorded here because the doctrinal fit is close enough to tempt.

A five-word run with opposite polarity. Proverbs 10:3 is a promise — 'The LORD will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish' — where the verb governs a harm God prevents. Ether 8:22 is a threat: 'the Lord will not suffer that the blood of his saints … shall always cry unto him from the ground … and yet he avengeth them not', where the verb governs a delay God will not extend. The KJV construction 'the LORD will not suffer' is the ordinary way of saying God will not permit something, and the two verses do not permit the same thing. The real sources of this verse are Genesis 4:10 and Revelation 6:10, catalogued as a link here.

A five-word run of judgment boilerplate. Psalm 92:7's wicked spring as the grass and flourish only 'that they shall be destroyed for ever'; Ether 8:22's nation that upholds secret combinations 'shall be destroyed'. The clause is the KJV's standard predicate for the fate of the wicked and the Book of Mormon's too — it is the burden of the whole book of Ether and of Moroni's editorial voice throughout. No content word beyond the verb is shared and the Psalm's grass image, which is what makes the Psalm distinctive, is absent.

'Yea, even the sword of the justice of the eternal God, shall fall upon you, to your overthrow and destruction.' The image is unmistakably scriptural and Deuteronomy 32:41-43 is its likeliest biblical home — 'If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment, I will render vengeance to mine enemies' — the more so because Deuteronomy 32:43, 'he will avenge the blood of his servants', stands behind the vengeance language of the preceding verse. But 'sword of the justice' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses, and the sword of God's justice is a Book of Mormon fixture rather than a King James one: Alma 26:19, Alma 60:29 and Helaman 13:5 all have it, and Moroni is using the book's own phrase. Declined as a biblical link for want of any shared string; recorded so that a reader who reaches for Deuteronomy 32 is told why the catalogue did not.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 4:1-12 at this verse alongside Genesis 3:1-7, and the reference is a fair one for a study edition: Ether 8:25 says the devil 'hath caused man to commit murder from the beginning', which is a summary of Cain. But this catalogue puts links where the wording is (CONVENTIONS §6a), and the Cain material of Ether 8 is verbal in two other places. At 8:15 Cain is named outright and the predicate attached to him, 'a murderer from the beginning', is a five-word KJV singleton — from John 8:44, not from Genesis 4. At 8:22 and again at 8:24 the blood of the slain cries from the ground for vengeance, which is Genesis 4:10 verbatim in its distinctive words ('blood crieth' is a KJV singleton), and mediation-check.py confirms Ether has the Genesis form rather than Hebrews 12:24's. Both are catalogued as links. Ether 8:25 itself reaches Cain through a summary phrase with no Genesis wording in it, so the row is discharged here by cross-reference: a reader sent to this verse by Hardy should go to 8:15 for Cain and to 8:22 for Abel's blood. The Genesis 3 half of Hardy's row is answered by the link at this verse, with the note that the verbal contact is at Genesis 3:13 rather than in 3:1-7.

'That they may come unto the fountain of all righteousness and be saved.' 'Fountain of' occurs in fifteen KJV verses and the metaphorical ones are well distributed — the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13), of life (Psalm 36:9, Proverbs 13:14, Proverbs 14:27), of Jacob, of Israel, of tears. None of them is a fountain of righteousness, and no KJV verse joins the noun to that abstraction. The Book of Mormon does it three times — 1 Nephi 2:9, where Lehi wishes Laman were 'continually running into the fountain of all righteousness', here, and again at Ether 12:28 — so Ether 8:26 is drawing on Lehi's phrase rather than on any one biblical fountain. Recorded to show that the candidate was considered and to say where the phrase actually comes from.
